candidates.original_title: Sex-role stereotypes and self-concepts in college students
candidates.description: Male and female college students agree about gender-typical traits and attribute more socially desirable traits to men than to women
candidates.citation_sentence: This study is a partial replication of the 1968 investigation by Rosenkrantz, Vogel, Bee, Broverman, and Broverman of gender stereotypes among college students.
candidates.notes: The paper calls this a 'partial replication' and reports both similarities to and differences from the original (fewer stereotypes found, reversed social desirability pattern). The original study's DOI is not provided in the paper, so original_url is left blank. The replication finds that gender stereotypes still exist (high agreement between men and women) but with fewer stereotypic items, and the social desirability finding is reversed (women's traits rated as more socially desirable, opposite of the original). The authors frame this as a partial replication with changes, making the overall result inconclusive rather than a clean reversal.

candidates.original_title: Sex-role stereotypes and self-concepts in college students
candidates.description: Students attribute more socially desirable traits to men than to women.
candidates.citation_sentence: This paper reports a partial replication of the study by Rosenkrantz, et al. (1968) aimed at clarifying whether changes have occurred in the content of gender stereotypes and the relative perceived social desirability of traits associated with men and with women since 30 years ago.
candidates.notes: The replication found the opposite pattern, with traits associated with the typical woman judged more socially desirable than traits associated with the typical man; the authors describe this as a contrast with the original finding but do not explicitly call it a reversal. candidates.original_title: Sex-role stereotypes and self-concepts in college students
candidates.description: Male and female students rate themselves as less different from the opposite-sex prototype than the typical man and typical woman are from each other.
candidates.citation_sentence: This paper reports a partial replication of the study by Rosenkrantz, et al. (1968) aimed at clarifying whether changes have occurred in the content of gender stereotypes and the relative perceived social desirability of traits associated with men and with women since 30 years ago.
candidates.notes: The authors report that the current participants showed the same self-rating pattern as participants in the original study, although the older male group was an exception on one comparison. [luna56: extra entry, not in the external record]
